Whether the BTA properly exercised its discretion, weighing the evidence and assessing the credibility of witnesses in connection with the valuation of the old Macy's building on Fountain Square. Faced with two competing appraisers, appraisals using similar methodologies, but with the city's appraiser, Mr. Thornton, relying on more data, the BTA weighed the testimony, weighed the evidence and adopted the appraisal that it determined was the more reliable of the two, the cities. Now for decades, recognizing the expertise that the BTA brings to these matters, Ohio Courts of Appeal have afforded the specialists who make up the Board of Tax Appeals a great deal of deference in making their decisions about real estate value determinations. One Ohio Supreme Court decision, this one from 2016, put it succinctly like this, and it's a short quote. Quote, if the parties present competing appraisals at the BTA, the weighing of evidence and the assessment of credibility are the statutory job of the BTA, and that body is vested with wide discretion, wide discretion in carrying out that function. As to the old Macy's site, the Board of Revision adopted the auditor's $19 million valuation, and so the parties wound up in front of the BTA with the school district defending the BOR decision and the city seeking a lower valuation. The city offered evidence from two knowledgeable witnesses, including an appraiser, Mr. Thornton, whose qualifications were stipulated to. And as it turned out, the BTA agreed with Mr. Thornton, who had valued the property at just a shade under $11 million, $10,990,000, and it rejected the valuation offered by the school district's appraiser, James Burt, of $16.73 million. They both agreed that the three-story structure would have to be redeveloped to achieve its highest and best use under the circumstances, and they both agreed that the underground parking garage beneath the building was worth $4.1 million. So, the dispute centers on the above-ground portion of the site itself and how it should be valued. And even there, the similarities in the appraisers' methodological approaches were quite similar. Both rejected the income and cost methodologies as unsuitable, and both used a sales comparison approach. They each selected a number of comparable properties. Mr. Thornton examined six. Mr. Burt examined four. Two of them, I think, were the same buildings. But at the end, the work of the two appraisers diverged with Mr. Thornton's valuation coming in at the $11 million figure and Mr. Burt's at the $16 million figure. And the main source of the disagreement there was whether extra floors could practically be added to the existing structure. So, in addition to Mr. Thornton's testimony, the city presented the testimony of Adam Gelter, no N, an executive with 3CDC, who testified for the city and provided some of the factual underpinnings that informed Mr. Thornton's work. Mr. Gelter testified, in part based on the results of engineering studies and other factors, that further construction of multiple floors was impractical for a host of reasons, including costs, building code issues, the footprint of the building, the north side being blocked by another building, the footprint of the building, and the practical difficulty of having heavy construction equipment in the Fountain Square area. So, Mr. Thornton and Gelter essentially saw adding multiple additional floors to the structure not only impractical but really functionally impossible. So, in other words, Mr. Gelter offered strong corroboration for Mr. Thornton's valuation of the property, and in the end, the BTA adopted Mr. Thornton's valuation over Mr. Burt's because he had better accounted for the value of the site and the cost of the necessary demolition and redevelopment. The Ohio Supreme Court and healthcare REIT, for one, found it sufficient for the BTA to simply say, we find one of the appraiser's opinions of value more persuasive, but the BTA did considerably more than that here, and before getting to its analysis, the BTA recited much of the evidence it had heard from Messrs.
